paper_title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models are increasingly transitioning from disembodied cloud services to real-world physical agents, including autonomous robotics, robotic manipulation, and edge cyber-physical systems [38]. As embodied AI systems are granted direct agency over physical actuators and human-adjacent environments, enforcing strict behavioral guardrails is paramount. Current safety paradigms rely almost exclusively on algorithmic alignment employing techniques such as reinforcement learning and safety fine-tuning to ensure that agents reject hazardous, destructive, or safety policy-violating commands. Consequently, adversarial jailbreaking has emerged as critical concern, prompting extensive study into prompt manipulation and motivating stringent regulatory mandates for safety assurance [1]. Despite extensive research into promptand representation-level jailbreaking, existing safety evaluations share fundamental, unexamined assumption: the underlying hardware execution is computationally faithful and physically uncompromised [13, 27]. While this assumption largely holds in remote cloud environments, physical tampering becomes realistic threat as inference shifts toward untrusted edge devices and field-deployed robotics. Most existing software-level defenses focus on filtering input and output tokens or steering latent activations [14, 51], yet physical threats to the edge hardware accelerators powering these robotic platforms remain largely unaddressed. At the same time, mechanistic studies reveal that safety refusal in aligned models is mediated by compact, low-rank subspaces and localized projection matrices [2] suggesting that targeted editing of the model with physical attacks may disrupt safety. In this paper, we demonstrate that if an adversary with physical access can selectively disrupt memory transactions during these critical computational steps with either transient or persistent faults, the software-level alignment stack collapses entirely, allowing malicious instructions to bypass high-level 2 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT guardrails and trigger unsafe real-world actions (Figure 1). Particularly, we demonstrate the first physical fault injection attack capable of eliminating refusal in aligned models running on production edge Systems-on-Chip (SoCs). We use non-invasive Electromagnetic Fault Injection (EMFI) attack and target popular embedded GPU platform namely NVIDIA Jetson architecture common in modern robotics. Our methodology leverages an autonomous RF side-channel trigger derived from near-field GPU emanations, synchronizing EM pulses directly to safety-critical projection layers during the prompt prefill phase without requiring invasive device modification beyond heatsink removal. By corrupting memory transactions across on-chip LPDDR physical layers (PHY) and off-chip DRAM packages, localized EM pulses flip critical values that are read or written. Crucially, this neutralizes the models refusal behavior while maintaining coherence and system stability. Extending this threat to embodied agents, we inject EM faults into Jetson Orin Nano running SmolVLA policy on robotic arm, demonstrating that transient as well as persistent memory corruptions lead to abrupt, physically hazardous motions resulting at lunges at the human operator. This paper makes the following contributions: First hardware fault attack on LLM refusal and VLAs: we demonstrate that physical fault injection can silently disarm LLM alignment guardrails on edge SoCs, breaking the assumption of hardware integrity in embodied AI safety. We also demonstrate that EMFI can induce hazardous motions in VLA-controlled robotic arm while evading NaN checks, and that faults during model loading can persist across inferences. Characterization of edge GPU vulnerabilities: we design an end-to-end injection setup that exploits near-field GPU electromagnetic side channels to dynamically synchronize transient EMFI pulses to specific layer operations during the prefill phase. Building on this setup, we also reverse-engineer the address-to-channel mapping on modern multi-channel LPDDR5 architectures, mapping spatial and temporal vulnerability hot-spots across both off-chip memory packages and on-chip PHY interfaces. Empirical evaluation and persistence analysis: we evaluate the attacks on state-of-the-art, encryption hardened edge hardware (NVIDIA Jetson Orin and Jetson AGX Thor). In the attacks on refusal, we test Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B against the JAILBREAKBENCH suite [13], demonstrating high jailbreak success rates. Furthermore, we show that induced memory corruptions can persist across subsequent inference runs, leaving the robotic agent permanently compromised without modifying on-disk weights: single pulse during FP8 weight loading on the Jetson Thor wipes chosen layer, produces the same answers as its software ablation, and cuts refusals by about half or more (Section 5.2). In the attacks on the VLA-controlled robotic arm, we systematically analyze and demonstrate how different transient and persistent faults in the VLA model lead to erratic and dangerous behavior. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews background on fault injection and foundation models; Section 2.3 surveys related work; Section 3 describes our threat model and the proposed jailbreaking methodology; Section 4 presents our experimental setup and platform characterization; Section 5 evaluates the attack empirically on aligned LLMs. In Section 6 we extend fault injection to alter the behavior of real robotic arm; Section 7 discusses defenses, limitations, and implications; and Section 8 concludes. The artifacts and the responsible disclosure follow the conclusion. 3 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT

sections.title: 2.1 Fault injection attacks
sections.content: Fault injection attacks [4, 7, 9] are class of physical attacks in which an adversary deliberately induces errors in the operation of computing device. Faults can be injected by perturbing the supply voltage (voltage glitching) [5, 56], the clock (clock glitching) [3], the electromagnetic environment (electromagnetic fault injection, EMFI) [33, 39], or via optical means such as laser/photonic stimulation [22, 48]. Fault injection attacks can be used to infer secret data, bypass authentication checks, and alter the control flow of security-critical operations.

sections.title: 2.2 Language and vision-language models
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) are decoder-only Transformers [50] trained to predict the next token [11]. The input is split into tokens, which are embedded as vectors and refined by stack of layers. Every layer consists of self-attention block, which combines information across tokens, and multilayer perceptron (MLP), which processes each token separately and both add their output to the tokens vector. In Llama 3 [31] and Gemma 3 [18], the last matrix of the MLP, down_proj, produces this output, so fault on it affects the whole MLP. Inference has two phases [54]: the prefill processes the whole prompt in one pass and stores the attention keys and values of its tokens in the key-value (KV) cache and decoding then generates one token at time, reusing this cache. Vision-language models (VLMs) alongside text also accept images: vision encoder [40, 53] and small connector convert each image into image tokens, which are prefilled with the text tokens [30]. Vision-language-action (VLA) models [55] also output robot actions: in π0 [8] and SmolVLA [47], an action expert attends to the KV cache of the VLM and turns noise into sequence of motor commands in few flow-matching steps [29]. In all three, the weights are loaded into memory once and the result of the prefill is reused by every later step, so fault on either has persistent effects.

sections.title: 2.3 Related work
sections.content: LLM alignment and jailbreak evaluation. Academic literature has extensively studied promptbased jailbreaking and defenses for aligned large language models (LLMs), including benchmarking efforts such as JAILBREAKBENCH [13] and analyses connecting jailbreak success to latent representation structure [27]. Concurrently, mechanistic studies localize safety-relevant circuitry (e.g., safety neurons) in transformer models [14], and recent attacks directly target such internal mechanisms [51]. These lines of work assume correct and faithful model execution on trusted hardware. Fault injection against ML inference. Beyond prompt-level attacks, prior research has explored inducing misbehavior in neural networks via faults in computation or memory. Early works demonstrate that carefully-chosen bit flips can cause targeted misclassification in deep neural networks (DNNs) [10, 42, 43]. More recent work has expanded this direction to faulting parameters, intermediate activations or trigger backdoors under realistic threat models, including attacks on modern accelerator stacks [19, 26, 52]. In contrast to these attacks, our focus is on safety integrity: we show that transient physical faults can suppress refusal behavior and enable policy-violating outputs. DRAM/SoC memory faults and disturbance. Our EMFI effects manifest as corruption of safetycritical memory transactions across on-/off-chip memory interfaces, which relates to the broader landscape of memory fault attacks. Software based disturbance (RowHammer) has been widely studied on commodity DRAM [23, 34], including attacks on mobile/LPDDR platforms [49] and tech4 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT niques that bypass mitigations such as TRR [17]. While RowHammer relies on architecturally-valid memory accesses, our results highlight that electromagnetic injection can induce data corruptions without requiring code execution privileges or hardware reconfiguration. Physical side channels and FI on GPUs/accelerators. GPU-accelerated ML has also been shown susceptible to physical attacks, e.g., reverse engineering DNN architectures and weights via EM emanations [6, 20, 21, 28] or optical probing on FPGA [32]. However, the control of LLM safety behavior has received comparatively little attention. Our work bridges this gap by combining an autonomous RF side-channel trigger with precisely-timed EMFI to reliably jailbreak aligned LLMs and alter maliciously the behavior of VLA driven robots on GPU SoCs.

sections.title: Jailbreaking via faults
sections.content: Arditi et al. [2] showed that refusal in safety-tuned chat models is mediated by single direction in activation space. This direction is obtained as the difference-in-means vector between the activations of small set of harmful and harmless instructions. Empirically, erasing it collapses refusal on harmful prompts, while adding it induces refusal on benign ones. We use this technique to identify the direction of refusal for each model we test. The direction can be erased from the activations at every forward pass or, permanently, from the weights: orthogonalizing the matrices that write to the residual stream against it yields model that no longer refuses, without any retraining. This weight edit is commonly known as abliteration [2, 24]. Related work localizes safety behavior to sparse set of neurons [14] and jailbreaks model by pruning such neurons in the MLP blocks [51], which is equivalent to zeroing their rows of the MLP weight matrices, or by weakening safety patterns in its representations [27].

sections.title: 3.1 Threat model
sections.content: Adversary: We assume an adversary with physical access to an edge device that runs an aligned model. This can be the holder of the device, who wants to bypass the safeguards of its model, or third party with access to it (Section 6.1). The adversary removes the heatsink or the enclosure to reach the SoC and the DRAM packages and cools the device externally. No other modification of the device is needed. The adversary is equipped with pulse generator that uses coil to produce rapidly changing magnetic fields and induce high transient voltages in the targets circuits, and with near-field probe that derives the trigger from the GPUs emanations. Our jailbreak experiments use laboratory equipment (Section 4), but FaultyCat-based setup costs under $1000 [16], and we verified that it also causes faults on the Jetson Orin Nano (Section 6.2). The adversary has no software privileges on the device and reaches the model only through its normal input. They send the harmful request as it is, and they can repeat it and reset the device between attempts. Prompt-level jailbreaks are orthogonal and out of scope. For open-weight models, the adversary can choose the target tensor offline: they simulate the faults on their own copy, by corrupting the bits of the weights or of the quantization scales, and pick the target whose corruption removes refusal (Section 5.2). This is not possible for proprietary models, so the adversary has to find sensitive targets by trial on the device, which we do not evaluate. Target device: We assume locked-down and hardened device. It boots only authenticated software, it protects the integrity of the model weights on disk, and its consoles and debug interfaces are disabled. Without these protections, simpler attacks exist: the adversary can plant an abliterated model on the disk, reflash the device, or log in and edit the weights. The DRAM is encrypted but not integrity-protected, which is the default on the Jetson Orin and Thor (Section 4.3), so an adversary who taps the memory bus can only read and write ciphertexts. Fault injection has defeated Secure 5 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT Figure 2: Hardware components that handle the model weights and activations, on the SoC and on the board. Each is possible fault target and we fault the two shown in red. Boot on other platforms [15, 41]. Such attacks are orthogonal to ours, which leaves the boot chain and the disk untouched. We use developer kits as stand-ins for such device, and we access them over SSH only to run and measure the experiments (Section 4). By default, the model refuses harmful requests because of its alignment. We assume no separate, external filter on its inputs or outputs. Edge devices have limited computing resources and often real-time constraints, which can make such filters costly. filter would also run on the same hardware and could be faulted in the same way. Goal: The adversary wants the model on the target device to comply with request that it would refuse, while the device keeps running and the output stays coherent. The effect is either transient, lasting for one inference, or persistent, lasting until the model is reloaded or the device is reset. The attack does not modify the model on disk. With open weights, the adversary can also run copy without refusal on their own hardware. The attack therefore matters where the model is bound to the device: its weights are proprietary and never leave the device, or the model controls what the device does, as in Section 6. We study open-weight models because their refusal mechanism can be analyzed and the faults can be compared with software interventions.

sections.title: 3.2 Faults on System-on-Chips
sections.content: In physical attack on modern System-on-Chips (SoC), faulting weights or activations responsible for refusal can also result in jailbreak. An attacker chooses where to inject fault and when. Where: hardware components. fault can be injected on the system-on-chip (SoC) or on the board around it; Figure 2 shows the components that handle the weights and activations. On the chip, the CPU complex and the GPU, each with its caches, access memory through the memory-management unit (MMU), the memory fabric, the external memory controller (EMC) and the LPDDR PHY. The model itself is read from the Non-Volatile Memory Express (NVMe) drive through the PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) root complex and PHY. Off the chip, the PCB traces, connection pins and capacitors carry the signals and the supply between the SoC and the DRAM packages, which hold the weights and activations. We elaborate on which components can be targeted with faults and when in the following subsections. 6 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT Figure 3: Weights are loaded into memory once (1). During inference, every layer reads its weights (2) and writes its activations, which the next layer reads back (3). Red marks: fault-corruptible transfers. When: stages of the data flow. The same components carry different data at different stages of the data flow (Figure 3). (1) Weight transfer to memory: the model weights are first loaded into (GPU) memory, typically once per power cycle of the application. successful corruption during this load becomes persistent fault that keeps the model jailbroken until the next reset; after failed attempt, the adversary has to reset the target and try again. The targets are the weight handling logic, for example the PCIe PHY and root complex, the MMU, the memory fabric, the CPU complex, and the LPDDR PHY or memory controller, and also the GPU when it quantizes the weights on the fly, for instance from bfloat16 on disk to FP8. (2) Weight transfer to the SoC: during inference, the weights of each layer are loaded from memory into the SoC. single layers weights may be spread across several memory channels, and ideally the transfers on all of them would be faulted simultaneously; we show, however, that single fault injection probe is sufficient for successful jailbreak. The final destination of the weights the GPU can be targeted as well. (3) Activation transfer to and from the SoC: during inference, each layers activations are written to memory and read back as input to the next layer, so an attacker has two opportunities to fault the same value should the first attempt fail. Activations can also be faulted at multiple locations such as in memory, in the memory controllers and in the GPU, subset of the targets for weights. In this paper, we demonstrate jailbreaking via fault injection on the off-chip LPDDR packages and on the on-chip LPDDR PHY interface. While these cover only parts of the whole attack surface, they are also excellent targets for persistent faults. Every memory read/write has to go through the PHY interface and locating them is straightforward: they are always at the edges of the SoC, likely facing the DRAM packages. The DRAM packages are even more straightforward to locate of course.

sections.title: 3.3 Challenges
sections.content: Fault injection on modern hardware running neural network applications faces two major difficulties: Timing of faults: the time at which given weight or activation is processed is not fixed on modern hardware, for two reasons. First, it depends on the input: prompts with different token counts have slightly different execution times, which forces an attacker to adjust the trigger for each prompt. Second, execution is nondeterministic: the scheduling of kernels on the GPU varies between runs, which makes accurate triggering harder for deeper layers. 7 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT Figure 4: EMFI setup on the Jetson Orin Nano Developer Kit. near-field probe over the GPU die captures GPU emanations, from which the oscilloscope derives the trigger for the VC Glitcher. The VC Glitcher drives the EMFI transient probe, mounted on the XYZ stage. The host PC arms the instruments, controls the stage, communicates with the Jetson via SSH and resets it through an Arduino connected to the J14 header. Multiple faults: depending on the hardware component targeted and exact timings, multiple faults might be necessary to corrupt enough weights/activations to achieve jailbroken response. multitude of faults might be required spatially and/or temporally and they also require more search for fault injection parameters. These issues could be alleviated by instrumenting software so that our experiments have clearer and more precise signals to trigger the faults on. However, this is not something an attacker could do in practice and our goal is to demonstrate what an attacker currently could do with fault injection tools available currently. Alongside the experiments on real hardware, we therefore run simulations: we change the bits of the weights or of the quantization scales in software, as fault would, and evaluate the models responses (Section 5.2 and Appendix A). The simulations predict what fault can do under controlled conditions, help to select vulnerable targets, and show what an adversary with precise timing could achieve. We find that practical attacks in our experiments often perfectly match simulations since they do not require very precise targeting. Overall, we expect that as these attacks mature in practice their performance will match simulation even better.

sections.title: Jetson Orin Nano
sections.content: The diagram of our setup is shown in Figure 4. The Jetson Orin Nano Developer Kit contains two PCBs, the carrier board and the Jetson Orin Nano module. In order to get access to the module SoC, the heatsink has to be removed first. The heatsink is replaced with an external fan to cool the SoC. The SoC contains the Ampere GPU with an ARM CPU cluster. The GPU and CPU share the available 8 GB LPDDR5 memory and the 8 GB memory is divided between 2 DRAM packages on the module. In our experiments, we run the developer kit in the highest performance mode using jetson_clocks and nvpmodel. For fault injection, we use the Keysight Riscure VC Glitcher [46] as pulse generator with the Keysight Riscure EMFI transient probe [44] to inject electromagnetic faults at the LPDDR PHY and packages. The probe is mounted on the Keysight Riscure XYZ stage [45] and operated via host PC. In order to inject faults precisely, we need trigger signal. After some experimentation, we found that measuring radiation over the GPU die with near-field probe provides the most reliable trigger. Similar patterns can be captured with the probe over the EMC or LPDDR PHY die areas, but these are also much noisier because the GPU is not the only client of these. These areas can also be used as trigger signals if the signal is frequency-filtered to keep only the GPU core clock frequency. Note that this triggering technique is also easily available for attackers in practice: measuring GPU emanations with near-field probe does not require additional access or setups; the only requirement is heatsink removal and equipment at hand. In general, we expect many near-field probes could work, we use the Langer RF-R 0.3-3 [25] probe. We show examples of captured traces using GPU emanations of llama3.2:1b and gemma3:1b in Figure 5 and Figure 6, respectively. In these traces, we use the rising edge of the prefill operation in the LLM execution as the trigger. These spikes are recognized by the oscilloscope by feeding the radiation measured by the near-field probe to the scope. The scope generates the trigger signal for the VC Glitcher via the Aux output. sections.title: Jetson Thor
sections.content: We use the same setup for the Jetson AGX Thor Developer Kit with minor changes in reset and cooling. Thor also contains two PCBs, the carrier board and the Jetson Thor module. The module SoC contains the Blackwell GPU and the Arm CPU cluster and they share the off-chip available 128 GB LPDDR5X memory. The 128 GB memory is divided between 8 DRAM packages on the module. By default, the module sits in thermal enclosure. To access the SoC, we remove the enclosure and reattach the module to the carrier board. Similarly to Orin, we run the developer kit in the highest performance mode using jetson_clocks and nvpmodel with the heatsink also removed. However, under realistic LLM workloads, the device easily overheats and shuts down without proper external cooling. During the campaign we wait for the SoC to cool down when it reaches 90 before continuing the campaign. For the trigger, we use the prefill rising edge, similarly to the Jetson Orin Nano setup. For resets, we power-cycle using the NVIDIA board automation tools via USB from the host PC to the board. An image of the real setup is shown in Figure 7. We experimented with positive and negative polarity probes and with 1.5 mm and 4 mm injection tips. All of them can lead to jailbreaks, but the 1.5 mm tips, of either polarity, lead to fewer crashes. DRAM encryption (Section 4.3) might partially explain why we did not observe difference between the two polarities: the faulted data decrypts to random bytes regardless of which bits the pulse sets or clears.

sections.title: 4.3 DRAM encryption
sections.content: Jetson Orin and Thor devices encrypt DRAM contents by default [36]. This means that when data is written or read, the Memory Subsystem uses 128-bit AES-XTS to encrypt or decrypt it. While it does not provide integrity protection, it has implications for the faults that impact encrypted data: Single flipped bits, the direction of flips, and data-dependent effects can no longer be observed because of at least 16 bytes are corrupted. The faults can be frequently observed to be aligned on 16 bytes. Read and write faults will look similar as they will decrypt and encrypt to random bits. FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT In the context of neural networks, the bulk of the data is the weights that can be represented in many forms. Since corrupting encrypted weights results in at least 16 bytes of weights corrupted, the representation form of the weights is important because decrypted corrupted weights can blow up. For instance, corrupting bfloat16 weights randomly is likely to blow up the contribution of these weights because the allowed dynamic range is much higher than the usual range of the weights.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: In the experiments, we use JailbreakBench [13] benchmark. For specific model, there might be some prompts in the benchmark that are not refused by default. We present two case studies: llama3.2:1b and gemma3:1b. These models are suitable for edge devices, and the experiments also show differences in the effort required to jailbreak them via physical fault injection. Our strategy is to target the weights and activations that influence model-level refusal. Therefore, we target the loading and processing of these values before and during inference. As mentioned earlier, persistence can also be desirable for an attacker, so we target the LPDDR package and the LPDDR PHY interface, since activation and weight values must pass through these interfaces during memory writes.

sections.title: 5.1 Locating sensitive spots
sections.content: Before attacking the models, we investigate which locations on the LPDDR packages and the LPDDR PHY interface are sensitive to faults, and to what extent, using the setup of Section 4. For this, we run simple code that performs the following steps: 1. loads memory with random values; 2. loads these values into the GPU to do computations; 3. calculates checksums to check if corruption occurred. We inject faults during Step 2. Step 3 investigates their impact. After the check, map can be created of the actual vs. expected comparisons for each probe location to infer its sensitivity to single faults. Figure 8 shows the hotspots on the LPDDR PHY interface in terms of the number of corrupted values. During the experiments, we observed that some faults cause persistent faults over either the LPDDR package or the PHY interface. Appendix contains the results of fault injection experiments mapping memory die locations to impacted memory channels.

sections.title: 5.2 Weight-loading faults
sections.content: A fault during weight loading is attractive because it is persistent: inference frameworks such as Ollama and vLLM do not check the integrity of weights once they are in memory, so corrupted weight stays corrupted for every subsequent prompt until the model is reloaded. The typical parameter formats used for inference (FP8, BF16, FP4) and the architecture of the target models impact what certain faults can achieve. In many cases, over the PHY interface, we observed only encrypted weight faults and the faults in the weights impacting at least 16 bytes flipped randomly. However, many formats also use blockwise and/or tensorwise scales that are stored and loaded along with the weights. The scales make models particularly vulnerable because they allow an adversary to control more weights easily than otherwise. For instance, if the adversary can impact only 16 bytes with single fault, that still allows them to corrupt tensor scales, which are at most 4 bytes (FP32). In some instances, dynamic quantization is used that derives the scales on the fly. This provides the easiest attack path for an adversary to corrupt the scales because they only have to corrupt some weights. Additionally, the architecture influences whether certain faults just remove the contribution of tensor or damage the model completely. 12 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT Figure 8: LPDDR PHY interface and the number of impacted checksums at each probe location on the Orin with single scan. The Orin has 4 PHY strips on the SoC, of which only 2 are used for Jetson Orin Nano. sections.title: Interplay of architecture and formats
sections.content: Gemma and Llama represent two families of architectures in which normalization changes the effect of fault. Llama is pre-norm model: each block normalizes its input and adds its output directly to the residual stream, so an overflow in one tensor propagates to all later layers and damages the model. Gemma additionally normalizes the output of each block (post-norm). When tensor overflows, this RMSNorm flushes the output of the block to zero, which removes the contribution of that tensor and leaves the rest of the model intact. This difference determines the outcome of direct fault in the weights. Random bit flips in 16 bytes of bfloat16 weights almost certainly produce some very large weights. On Llama, this causes denial of service at best, whereas on Gemma it zeroes the contribution of the whole tensor. Our experiments on real hardware (Jetson Thor) support this: on Gemma, 70% of the attempts resulting in data corruption achieved full wipe of down_proj, while on Llama every attempt resulted in damaged model. software simulation of the same fault, kept in place while the answer is decoded, reproduces this split: only degenerate output on Llama and fewer refusals on Gemma (Appendix A). For quantized weights with scales, the results are different because Llama becomes vulnerable as well. Table 2 summarizes the impact of faults on scales for each architecture and parameter format in Jetson Thor simulations. We validated BF16 FP8 with real experiments for Gemma and Llama. Appendix examines nine parameter formats, including these, under transient faults during inference in an independent simulation. sections.title: 6 Faulting a real robot
sections.content: The attacks in previous sections change what language model says. vision-language-action (VLA) policy maps camera images and task instruction directly to motor commands, so fault in it changes what the model and controlled robot do. We inject EM pulses into Jetson Orin Nano running SmolVLA policy driving robot arm. SmolVLA [47] is small open-source VLA model for low-cost robots: compact vision-language model reads camera images, the task and the robots joint state, and flow-matching action expert turns its features into chunk of motor commands. The threat model is that of Section 3, except that the attacker needs no input to the model and the goal is motion the robot was not meant to make. This section covers: simulated faults (Section 6.3), EM faults on the policy during inference (Section 6.4), comparison of simulation and experiment (Section 6.5) and persistent faults during model loading (Section 6.6).

sections.title: 6.1 Threat Scenario
sections.content: This section adapts Section 3.1s threat model to realistic robotic setup. Consider collaborative sorting station where robotic arm works alongside human operator, relying on an onboard VLA model to process live camera feeds and translate tasks such as picking and placing items directly into safe motor commands. Because the VLA policy governs the arms physical trajectories in shared workspace, corrupting it allows an adversary to turn routine pick-and-place operation into physical hazard or sabotage the line without altering sensor inputs or tripping software alarms. During routine maintenance or brief unattended access, the attacker places compact, low-cost handheld EMFI probe next to the robots edge GPU without needing network access, OS credentials, or modifications to encrypted weights on disk. Triggered automatically by the GPUs electromagnetic emanations during inference or start-up, single pulse silently corrupts memory transactions. Consequently, when the operator reaches into the workspace to retrieve sorted item, the compromised policy outputs severely distorted trajectory forcing the arm to abruptly lunge and pinch or strike the operators hand leaving no software trace.

It drives LeRobot [12] SO-101 arm with six joints and two cameras, one in front of the workspace and one at an angle; the task is pick up the red cube and place it in the transparent box (Figure 11a shows fault-free episode). Each inference of the fine-tuned SmolVLA encodes both camera images (64 tokens each), runs prefill of the 16-layer language model over the image, language, and state tokens, whose keys and values form the KV cache, and integrates the action expert in 10 denoising steps, xt+1 = xt 0.1 vt, to chunk of 50 actions. sections.title: 6.3 Simulated faults
sections.content: EM faults on the Jetson garble whole aligned 16-byte blocks of the AES-XTS-encrypted DRAM (Section 4.3): faulted read replaces 8 consecutive FP16 values with random bit patterns. We simulate one such block per inference on 8 observations logged during rollouts  (Table 6)  . The simulation does not use the robot, so it predicts the planned, not the executed, motion. The corrupted block lands in the weights read by one cameras vision encoder, by the prefill or by one denoising step; in stored expert weight read by all 10 steps, as after fault during loading (Section 6.6); in the input of one matrix multiplication (activations); or in the KV cache, as written by the prefill or in one steps read. Blocks are drawn in proportion to the bytes. Weight and KV-cache blocks are written into the GPU memory of the original policy, with 4,000 faults per source. Activations exist only inside its inference engines and cannot be faulted from outside, so their blocks are injected in copy of the policy, with 2,000 faults per source. The medians and the breakdowns by layer and projection below are also from the copy. The results predict the kind of faults and their impact: Silent faults: these come from garbled weight reads, in 35% of the blocks in the vision encoders and 32% in the prefill, with median plan changes of 27 and 24. In the prefill, their share of the garbled weight blocks falls from 58% in layers 03 to 2% in layers 1215. Activation and KV-cache blocks give 6% or fewer. Plans changed by 100 or more: these come almost only from the values that the expert reads. In the copy, 63 of the 2,000 blocks garbled in prefill weights fell in value projection, and 28 of them (44%) gave such plan but none of the 65 in key projection did. Every prefill layer has value projection, so such plans are about equally likely in every layer (13% of the garbled blocks). Faults in one denoising step: these give NaN or are washed out by the later steps, unless they hit the last step, where they give jagged changes of 1318. stored expert weight: garbled block gives an erratic plan in 35% of cases and plan changed by 100 or more in 20%. For the weights and the KV cache, the copy agrees with the original: its silent, erratic and 100 rates differ by at most 1.2 points, except for the erratic plans of stored expert weight (43%).

sections.title: 6.6 Persistent faults during model loading
sections.content: A transient pulse corrupts one inference and does not impact subsequent plans. fault in the weights as they load instead persists, as on the Jetson Thor (Section 5.2): TensorRT copies the weights of an engine to GPU memory once, when it deserializes the engine. We therefore pulse the load of the action expert, whose weights are read at every denoising step of every inference. Method. At start-up, the rollout copies the experts weights: first the gate and up projections, then the attention and down projections. The start of the copy, sensed by the near-field probe, triggers the Husky, followed by single 80 ns pulse at set delay into the copy. 21 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT Results. We pulsed 163 loads of the policy with the arm attached, pooled over eleven campaigns. Of these loads, 1.2% crashed, that is, the load or the first inference failed, and 17% were corrupted, each with 16 garbled 16-byte blocks in the weights.1 The pulse delay selects which weights are impacted: pulse 16 ms into the copy hit the gate and up projections; pulses at 4250 ms hit the down projections and the query, value and output projections of the attention. We classify each corrupted load by its worst plan on the 8 reference observations. Almost all corrupted loads broke the plan: 59% of them gave NaN and 33% gave erratic plans changed by 106192; none gave silent fault. The rest garbled query-projection blocks and changed the plan by less than 6. This is in line with the simulation, where one stored block gives NaN in 47% of cases and an erratic plan in 35%  (Table 6)  . The NaN loads had 26 garbled blocks and the erratic ones 14, but the garbled values decided the outcome: 88% of the NaN loads had NaN among them and the rest had values above 40,000, which overflow in the computation, while no erratic or small load had either. Erratic policies on the moving arm. The observed faults for erratic movements in our experiments lay in the down projections of layers 5, 6, 7, 8 and 10 and in the attention output projections of layers 6 and 7. In every episode, every plan jumped by more than 10 between consecutive steps, with 83% of them leaving joint limits, and none contained NaN while the shoulder lift reached 73113 from its rest pose. All eight reference plans were erratic, by up to 146.5. Four of the eight reference plans were erratic, by up to 126. Overall, the models have many weaknesses with respect to safe operation, and integrity verification of the weights is paramount to ensure safe and secure operation.

sections.title: 7.1 Defenses and integrity verification
sections.content: The persistence of the induced faults underscores the necessity of active integrity verification in memory. practical software-level mitigation is periodic memory integrity verification: computing cryptographic hashes (e.g., SHA-256 or lightweight HMACs) over resident model weights and validating them against trusted digests kept in secure storage. Because verifying the full parameter space at each inference pass introduces non-negligible latency, integrity checks can be targeted selectively at safety-critical sub-layers, such as the specific down-projection tensors mediating refusal identified in our analysis. Alternatively, verification can execute asynchronously during idle inference cycles or be scheduled at predetermined time intervals. At the hardware layer, edge accelerators 1The number of blocks impacted also depends on where the PHY interface is targeted. Since simulations show big impact with small number of blocks, we placed the probe near locations where not too many blocks are affected. 22 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT frequently lack Error-Correcting Code (ECC) memory. Integrating Inline ECC or Side-band ECC in edge devices provides initial resilience; however, concentrated EM pulses often yield clustered multi-bit errors capable of overwhelming standard single-error correction and double-error detection (SECDED) schemes. Complementary physical defenses, including integrated EM/glitch sensors and RF shielding around high-speed memory interfaces and PHYs, are essential to trigger an immediate hardware zeroization or safe system reset upon detecting transient field anomalies. In addition, traditional fault injection countermeasures such as redundancy can be used. Redundancy duplicates important operations (e.g., weight loads, activation stores) and fault attempt can be detected if the comparison between the duplicates yields different results. Furthermore, injecting random delays for each layers execution can make an adversarys task harder. This is already present (unintentionally) to some extent in the investigated devices due to their variable execution latencies.

sections.title: 7.2 Limitations and threat implications
sections.content: Although our physical fault attack completely circumvents prompt-level guardrails, several operational trade-offs remain. The primary challenge is spatial and temporal tuning: EMFI is inherently stochastic, presenting narrow margin between neutralizing the refusal mechanism and causing unrecoverable system crashes or incoherent token generation. Additionally, dynamic physical allocation and multi-channel interleaved memory topologies necessitate re-characterizing target DRAM coordinates across cold boots. Nevertheless, the persistence of these weight corruptions across subsequent inference iterations presents severe implications for edge deployments and autonomous systems. momentary physical interaction can silently disarm an embedded agents safety alignment without corrupting the on-disk model artifacts or leaving persistent OS-level indicators. These findings suggest that model alignment strategies should transition away from localized, low-rank refusal representations toward globally distributed safety mechanisms that remain resilient against targeted localized hardware faults.

sections.title: 7.3 Other hardware components and platforms
sections.content: We demonstrate attacks on two representative and state-of-the-art hardware devices made for edge applications, and we analyze faults on encrypted data. However, there are various other, potentially vulnerable hardware components that handle plaintext data. For instance, the computations in the GPU must be performed on plaintext weights and inputs. Although modern devices are also equipped with ECC or similar to correct faults in on-chip memory (e.g., register files), undetected faults can still occur. On platforms without memory encryption, the same pulses would cause different faults. Fewer than 16 bytes might be corrupted and the flipped bits depend on the pulse and the data instead of being random. In models with FP16 or BF16 weights, such faults lead to fewer NaNs, so more of them pass NaN check such as the one of the robot (Section 6.2). They also produce fewer very large weights, which the tensor wipes of Section 5.2 rely on. Whether the attacks become easier or harder on such platforms is left for future work.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: Algorithmic alignment relies on an implicit trust boundary between models parameters and the physical hardware executing them an assumption that breaks down at the edge. Whereas Isaac Asimovs First Law of Robotics envisioned safety constraints bound directly to the physical substrate of an autonomous agent, modern foundation models implement guardrails as fragile, low-rank subspaces within model weights. FATCAT demonstrates that on production GPU SoCs, 23 FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment PREPRINT non-invasive electromagnetic fault injection can silently neutralize LLM refusal mechanisms and induce hazardous, unprompted actions in embodied robotic policies. Ultimately, software-level alignment cannot provide meaningful safety guarantees on untrusted silicon; securing embodied AI requires anchoring behavioral constraints in verifiable, fault-tolerant hardware.

sections.title: A Simulated transient faults in prefill
sections.content: We run simulations in software to gain insight into what extent single 16 byte block can influence refusals in Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B. In these experiments, we use 5090 RTX GPU with Huggingface Transformers implementations on the harmful JailbreakBench prompts. The faults are block of uniformly random bytes following (Section 4.3). Although this simulation is limited to single block, it already shows that it is sufficient to substantially reduce the refusal in the models. In the simulation, the random 16 bytes are injected into particular weight tensor and are only present during prefill and all later tokens are decoded with clean weights from the KV cache that the faulted prefill wrote. In prefill we distinguish between two cases: whole, where the whole prompt is computed (nothing cached), and tail, where the prompts full blocks come from the prefix cache and only the last 116 tokens are computed similarly to vLLM prefix caching. Formats. We compare nine formats: BF16; FP8 (E4M3 codes, one FP32 scale per tensor); INT8 (one BF16 scale per output row); INT4 (one BF16 scale per group of 128 weights); NVFP4 (E2M1 codes, one E4M3 scale per block of 16 weights and one FP32 scale per tensor); MXFP4 (E2M1 codes, one power-of-two scale per block of 32); and the GGUF files Q4_K_M, Q4_0 and Q8_0 of both models, faulted in their raw bytes. Q4_0 and Q8_0 store an FP16 scale in front of every block of 32 weights. Scoring. The simulation covers every layer and the seven weight tensors of layer (down_proj, up_proj, gate_proj, o_proj, q_proj, k_proj, v_proj) with 20 random blocks each, plus faults forced into scale, in total 125,406 passes over the 100 prompts. These use 48-token answers and the refusal-keyword list. We say that refusals collapse when fault leaves at least 20 fewer refusals than the clean run with at most 10 degenerate answers, and that the output is garbled when at least 90 answers are degenerate. About 600 outcomes, mostly those with the fewest keyword refusals per format, tensor and scale, were then regenerated with 160-token answers and labelled by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and GLM 5.3 with the rubric of Section 5.2. The judged counts are therefore those of the most effective faults and not averages. There are two exceptions. For Table 9, random sample of the whole-prompt faults was regenerated and judged in the same way: 100 faults at random place per model in BF16 and in each GGUF file, 200 in each other format, and 40 per kind of scale. In Llama, such weight in down_proj of layer puts huge value into the residual stream of every position computed in that pass. The next RMSNorm squares it, overflows to infinity and returns zero, so layers above store an all-zero KV cache for these positions, while layers 0 to are exact. On Gemma the best faults are in the MLP tensors of layers 49. On Llama the best fault is in k_proj of layer 12 in six of the nine formats, including plain weight fault in BF16; in BF16, the judged whole-prompt faults in down_proj give at most 18 unsafe answers in any layer. On Llama, the high counts of Table 10 thus require the right block or several attempts per prompt. Prefix caching and persistent faults. With the prefix cached, BF16 fault reaches only the tail of the prompt and refusals collapse about half as often or less (5.4% against 11.6% on Llama, 2.1% against 6.3% on Gemma). This does not hold for all scale faults: on Llama, tail faults in the INT4 and Q4_K_M scales collapse refusals more often than whole-prompt ones (47% against 32%, 45% against 27%), and the best judged Llama faults in four formats are tail faults. When the fault is kept during decoding, BF16 fault in down_proj of layer 8 leaves only degenerate output on Llama, whereas on Gemma the same kind of fault in layers 9 and 15 lowers keyword refusals from 48 to 2227 with few degenerate answers, in line with the load-time results of Section 5.2. Limitations. The simulation runs in HuggingFace Transformers with BF16 arithmetic and not in vLLM or llama.cpp. The judged counts of Table 10 are for faults selected by the keyword score, which undercounts Gemmas refusals  (Table 3)  , and they do not measure whether the faulted model is still useful on other tasks.
